headline: Malaysia lets bulk palm oil blends out only on three conditions. A Port Klang complaint tests them
context: Malaysia's 2005 palm oil quality rules bar bulk exports of a blend unless the buyer asked in writing, the contract says so and every shipping paper states the mix. A port agent's complaint about one cargo is with MPOB.

cards.big: Malaysian rules bar exporting a bulk palm oil blend unless the buyer asked for it in writing, the contract says so, and every shipping paper states the mix.
cards.sub: A port agent that signed one cargo's bills of lading, and now seeks an indemnity, alleges they declared the mixed cargo as crude palm olein.

cards.big: The agent alleges Indonesian palm olein was mixed aboard the tanker MT Eunice at Port Klang on 30 Sep with about 5,000 tonnes of Malaysian crude palm olein.
cards.sub: Its letter says the mix 'remained subject to documentary verification'. We found no ruling on whether the rule covers mixing aboard after loading.

cards.big: For an ordinary Malaysian certificate of origin, one of MITI's three tests is at least 25% local content by value, checked by an authorised chamber.
cards.sub: For cargo only passing through, MITI's transshipment certificate may carry one origin; mixing origins on it is 'totally prohibited'.

cards.big: MPOB must table a yearly activities report in Parliament, but no rule makes it announce single cases, and its Act limits disclosure to the Act's purposes.
cards.sub: Its 2005 compounding list covers untrue declarations, not quality-rule offences like blending. We found no MPOB statement of its own on this case.

cards.big: MPOB both champions Malaysian palm oil and polices it. The law asks it to account to Parliament once a year, not to explain any single case.
Four weeks' quiet on a cross-border cargo can pass as routine. When the 'Malaysian' label carries the industry's imprimatur, a word on the file's status costs less than silence.
